title: Microsoft AI chief says the company beat OpenAI's models, using less compute
content:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman told employees an in-house model was better than a similar offering from OpenAI, one of the software giant's biggest customers and partners.
"We now have a stronger pre-trained base model than the model that currently powers GPT 5.6 Sol," Suleyman said during a town hall meeting with employees on Thursday. "And in fact, we used one-quarter of the compute that OpenAI used to train their model."
Pre-training is the first stage of building an AI model, when it learns patterns from huge amounts of text, images, and other information. This takes massive amounts of expensive computing power, so Microsoft could save money if it's worked out a way to do this more efficiently.
Microsoft announced the model, MAI-Base-2, earlier on Thursday.
Suleyman said Microsoft privately tested this model against OpenAI models, including one nicknamed "Spud" that powers GPT-5.6. He added that Microsoft's model performed better on tests measuring how well AI can understand and predict patterns in information.
The comparisons are based on technical information Microsoft has about OpenAI's models, Suleyman said.
"Privately and confidentially, we've also compared it to the OpenAI models," Suleyman told employees, while suggesting that Microsoft has special access to information on how OpenAI models perform.
It's notable that Suleyman would choose to highlight limitations of OpenAI models, even in private discussions. Microsoft has invested billions of dollars in OpenAI, and owns a stake in the startup that is likely worth more than $100 billion. Any criticism of OpenAI could potentially dent the value of this huge investment.
The two companies also have a major partnership, with Microsoft offering OpenAI models to its Azure cloud customers. Microsoft has used OpenAI models for its own products such as Copilot, too.
But the relationship between the two companies has frayed in the past year or so. Increasingly, Microsoft has tried to branch out from OpenAI, including by working on its own models.
Suleyman also said Microsoft's new AI model used "12 times less computation than was used for DeepSeek, for example, on compute efficiency."
Suleyman didn't specify which DeepSeek model, but a public blog post described the pre-training of MAI-Base-2 being a lot more efficient than a similar offering from the Chinese lab, called DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base.
Microsoft in March created a new combined team for its commercial and consumer Copilot products and reassigned Suleyman to focus on building AI models in the company's superintelligence unit.
Microsoft declined to comment and OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

report.summary: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman says in-house MAI-Base-2 outperforms OpenAI's GPT-5.6 base model while using one-quarter of the training compute.
report.background: Microsoft and OpenAI have a deep but increasingly complicated relationship. Microsoft has invested billions in OpenAI, holds a stake reportedly worth more than $100 billion, sells OpenAI models through Azure, and uses them in Copilot. OpenAI has relied on Microsoft's cloud and capital. Yet as both companies expand, Microsoft has pushed to build its own models and reduce dependence on a partner that is also a competitor. The MAI-Base-2 announcement fits that strategy. Pre-training foundation models is extremely expensive, so claims about compute efficiency matter commercially as well as technically. The comparison also comes amid fierce efficiency competition, exemplified by DeepSeek's low-cost models, which have pressured US labs to show they can train strong models with fewer chips and less spending.
key_points: Suleyman told employees that MAI-Base-2 is a stronger pre-trained base model than the one powering OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. He said Microsoft's model performed better on tests measuring pattern understanding and prediction, though the comparison relied on Microsoft's private technical information about OpenAI's models rather than independent public benchmarks.

Microsoft says MAI-Base-2 was trained with one-quarter of the compute OpenAI used for its comparable model. Suleyman also claimed 12 times better compute efficiency than a DeepSeek model, which a company blog post identified as DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. Lower training costs could make Microsoft's models cheaper to develop and serve.

The remarks are strategically notable because Microsoft is OpenAI's biggest backer and a major cloud partner. Criticizing OpenAI's models, even privately, could complicate a partnership that has already frayed as Microsoft develops in-house alternatives and OpenAI seeks more independence.

Microsoft announced MAI-Base-2 the same day and has reorganized around AI model building, including a superintelligence unit led by Suleyman. Microsoft declined to comment and OpenAI did not respond, leaving the performance and efficiency claims unverified by outside researchers.
report.impact: If Microsoft's claims hold up, the AI race shifts further toward compute efficiency, not just raw scale. A model that matches or beats frontier baselines with a fraction of the training compute could lower costs for Microsoft's Copilot products and Azure customers, and increase pressure on OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and DeepSeek to publish efficiency gains. Developers would gain more model choices and potentially lower API prices, but they should treat vendor-private benchmarks cautiously until independent evaluations are available. For regular users, the nearer-term effect is likely cheaper or faster AI features in Microsoft products rather than a dramatic capability jump. The bigger story is the Microsoft-OpenAI alliance becoming more competitive.
report.tools: To follow the claims, watch Microsoft's MAI model family and Azure AI Foundry's model catalog, where new models often appear for testing. Compare public benchmarks via Hugging Face model cards and evaluation harnesses such as EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness or OpenAI Evals. DeepSeek's released models and technical reports offer a useful efficiency baseline. For enterprise trials, Azure AI Foundry and GitHub Models can be used to test cost and latency, but insist on reproducible, independent evals before switching production workloads.
